# Follow-up: quadratic duplicate-key scan in redact

Repo: entireio/cli. Worktree: /Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/worktree-rapid-forest-ef5e
Origin: PR #2321 (merging now). This is a tail-latency follow-up, not a correctness bug.

## What

PR #2321 added duplicate-JSON-key detection to redaction. `hasDuplicateJSONKeys` /
`tokenStreamHasDuplicateKeys` in `redact/redact.go` walk the token stream of EVERY parsed
JSONL line and compare each object key against the keys seen so far with
`slices.Contains(seen, k)` — O(k^2) in one object's key count.

Why the scan exists (keep this property, do not remove it): encoding/json keeps only the
LAST duplicate key, so a secret in a shadowed value is invisible to both the splice
collection and the post-splice verification while still sitting in the raw text. Lines with
duplicate keys are therefore rebuilt structurally instead of spliced.

## Measured (M4 Max, `-benchtime 5x -count=3`), pre-#2321 -> post-#2321

| input                                   | before  | after   | ratio |
|-----------------------------------------|---------|---------|-------|
| 2000 prose lines, ~8 keys each          |  81 ms  |  86 ms  | 1.06x |
| one object, 200 keys                    | 0.56 ms | 0.61 ms | 1.09x |
| one object, 2 000 keys                  | 5.7 ms  | 8.2 ms  | 1.45x |
| one object, 8 000 keys                  |  23 ms  |  66 ms  | 2.9x  |
| one object, 50 000 keys                 | 0.16 s  | 1.53 s  | 9.5x  |

Throughput was flat before (12.3 / 12.8 / 12.9 / 11.5 MB/s across those sizes); after it
degrades 11.1 / 8.7 / 4.4 / 1.26 MB/s. That curve is the quadratic, not noise.

## Two separable items

1. THE FIX — the quadratic tail. Stay on the slice for small objects (~16 keys) and switch
   to a lazily-allocated map above that. This preserves the property the current comment is
   protecting ("transcript objects carry a handful of keys, and a map allocation per object
   would be paid on every parsed line") while killing the tail. Real-world trigger is one
   wide map arriving as a tool result: `npm ls --json`, a coverage report keyed by file, a
   metrics dump, a flattened config export.

2. PROBABLY LEAVE — the scan is unconditional: it runs on every parsed line whether or not
   anything was flagged, unlike `ensureReplacementsLanded` which is gated on
   `len(repls) > 0`. That is the flat ~6% row. Defensible for the guarantee it buys; just
   worth a sentence in the PR so nobody re-derives it later.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than filing

The hooks run under wall-clock budgets (`gitrepo.StatusWalkBudget`, Codex's 3s
`agent.SessionEndBudgeter`). A wide-map line turns into a KILLED hook and a lost
checkpoint, not merely a slow Stop. Redaction is already documented in CLAUDE.md as ~99.7%
of the blob write.

## Suggested PR shape

- The map-above-threshold fix in `tokenStreamHasDuplicateKeys`.
- A committed benchmark over key counts (e.g. `BenchmarkJSONLContent_WideObject` with
  200/2 000/8 000 sub-benchmarks) — nothing currently pins the scaling, which is exactly
  why this regression was invisible to CI.
- Verify output is unchanged: `redact/jsonl_splice_verify_test.go` already covers the
  duplicate-key cases (`TestJSONLContent_RedactsSecretShadowedByDuplicateKey`,
  `...NestedDuplicateKey`, `...SingleJSONValueDuplicateKeyIsRebuilt`). They must stay green.

## Checked already, do not re-investigate

- Recursion depth in `tokenStreamHasDuplicateKeys` is fine: probed 9 000 / 9 999 / 10 001 /
  50 000 nesting levels through `JSONLContent`, no panic, no stack problem.
- The splice-verification pass itself (`ensureReplacementsLanded`) is free — it is gated on
  `len(repls) > 0` and measured within noise. Not the problem.

## Repo gates before commit

commit b629cccbae152a01e64f85d243805cfa2a9b4c76
Author: Stefan Haubold <stefan@entire.io>
Date:   Thu Aug 27 20:45:49 2026 +0200

    fix(redact): stop a JSONL replacement silently no-opping with the secret intact
    
    applyJSONReplacements detected on the decoded leaf but rewrote the raw bytes
    by searching for Go's re-encoding of that leaf. When a producer spelled the
    string differently the search matched nothing, the substitution did nothing,
    and the line was returned UNCHANGED WITH THE SECRET INTACT -- no error, no
    fallback, no log. Detection had worked; only substitution failed, silently.
    
    No attacker is needed. Node's JSON.stringify does not escape U+2028/U+2029
    while Go's encoder does, and Claude Code, Gemini CLI, opencode and Copilot CLI
    are all Node-based; those separators arrive routinely in text pasted from Word,
    PDFs or minified JS. PHP's json_encode emits \/ by default. A streaming chunk
    boundary that splits a surrogate pair leaves a lone surrogate, which decodes to
    U+FFFD and can never re-encode to itself. Invalid UTF-8 does the same. In an
    agent transcript one "text" leaf routinely holds a whole tool output, so a
    stray separator sharing a leaf with a secret is ordinary. Granularity is
    per-leaf: a trigger character elsewhere on the line does not save the secret's
    own leaf.
    
    Resolve each replacement against the string literals actually present in the
    raw text, matching on their DECODED value, so no producer's escaping choices
    are involved. A literal is located by byte offset and spliced, which keeps the
    rewrite byte-preserving -- a line with nothing to redact, and the untouched
    remainder of a line that has something, come back byte for byte. Re-serialising
    the parsed value would also have closed the hole, but it rewrites every line's
    formatting, which the incremental redaction cache and the
    CheckpointTranscriptSize growth baseline are built on top of; it would also
    collapse a pretty-printed opencode export onto one line, drop duplicate JSON
    keys, and turn a 19-digit id into 1.2345678901234568e+18.
    
    Matching is a superset of what the raw-byte substitution reached, so nothing
    that was redacted before stops being redacted: keyed replacements stay scoped
    to values under their own key (which is what keeps a skipped field's identical
    value intact) and keyless ones still match any literal. A keyed replacement now
    wins over a keyless one for the same literal rather than the outcome following
    the order repls arrive in, which is Go's randomized map iteration order.
    
    Every replacement is derived from a parse of the same text, so having no
    literal to land on is unreachable; it is still checked, and it is an error
    rather than output that claims to be redacted.
    
    redact/jsonl_encoding_test.go covers the leak end to end: 12 raw-encoding
    variants, all of which leak on main. redact/jsonl_literals_test.go pins the
    literal scanner's key/value classification and that a literal decoded on its
    own matches the whole-document decode -- the equivalence the match rests on.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Entire-Checkpoint: 01M128NTDCRK1CG1Y711GEE89V

content.text:
The current hybrid approach is the right tradeoff. Two possible refinements:

1. **Avoid one wasted slice growth at key 17.** Switch to the map before appending the 17th key. Currently `append` may grow capacity from 16 to 32 immediately before the slice is discarded.
2. **Add a focused scanner benchmark** for `hasDuplicateJSONKeys`, alongside the end-to-end `JSONLContent` benchmark, to isolate future duplicate-scan regressions from parser/redactor changes.

I would apply #1. I would only add #2 if maintainers want diagnostic benchmarks; the committed end-to-end benchmark already pins user-visible scaling. A custom raw-byte JSON scanner or unconditional map would add complexity/allocation without a demonstrated benefit.
how is the line drawn with 17?

The threshold is **16 unique keys per object**:

- Keys 1–16 use linear `slices.Contains`.
- A duplicate among those keys is detected immediately.
- On the 17th unique key, all 17 keys are copied into a map.
- Every subsequent key uses constant-time map lookup.
- Each nested object tracks its keys independently.

Why 16: small transcript objects avoid a map allocation, while the slice performs at most 120 prior-key comparisons across 16 unique keys. Beyond that, quadratic growth starts becoming less attractive. It follows the brief’s suggested “~16”; it was not independently tuned.

One implementation detail worth improving: currently the 17th key is appended before migration, potentially growing the slice unnecessarily. We can migrate before that append and insert the 17th key directly into the map.
can you explain that more?
ok, do it

Done and amended into `b6a54ee3c`.

The 17th unique key now goes directly into the newly allocated map, avoiding unnecessary slice growth and copying.

All required checks passed again:

- `mise run fmt`
- `mise run lint`
- `mise run test:ci`

Working tree is clean.

1. The one line that makes it correct is untested

I deleted the three-line loop that copies pre-threshold keys into the new map, and the entire redact suite still passes.

With it deleted, here's what actually happens — a 25-key object whose early k0 is duplicated at the end, shadowing a secret:

hasDuplicateJSONKeys missed a duplicate of a pre-migration key
shadowed secret shipped in certified output:
  {"k0":"REDACTED","k1":"filler 1",...

That is exactly the hole the duplicate-key scan was added to close, silently reopened, with green tests. Pi's real code passes this — the implementation is right, it just has no guard.

Why the new test misses it: TestHasDuplicateJSONKeys_WideObject duplicates key_19, the 20th key, which is already in the map by then — so it only exercises map-vs-map. Every pre-existing duplicate-key test has 2 keys and never crosses the threshold. Nothing covers a duplicate whose first occurrence was in the pre-migration slice. I have the test written and can drop it in.

2. The branch is based on a head that no longer exists

#2321 merged as 628169784, but its second parent is 7d947a313 — the branch got one more update before merge, so the e73fac296 pi built on isn't in main. The branch is currently 6 commits ahead of main and behind it on unrelated work (a large userdirs/tokenstore change landed since).

The content is identical, though: two-dot origin/main..b6a54ee3c shows only pi's own lines in redact (+15 test, 36± redact.go, +39 bench). So git rebase --onto origin/main e73fac296 replays just b6a54ee3c and drops the five #2321 commits as already-applied. Clean, but it has to happen before a PR.

Minor

- The benchmark uses "key_N":null values. That isolates the scan cleanly (29 MB/s vs 11 MB/s with string values) but under-measures a realistic wide object, where the regex layers run per leaf. Fine as a regression pin — worth a comment saying that's deliberate so nobody "fixes" it later.
- 50 000 keys — the case that showed 9.5× — isn't in the table. 8 000 catches a regression fine, so this is optional.
- const duplicateKeySliceThreshold = 16 is declared inside the case '{': block while the doc comment above the function refers to it by name; function scope would be easier to find.
